abstract: Chapter 1 of the OECD Employment Outlook 2026, published 2026-07-07. Its value to jobsdata.ai is that it is the most serious multi-country attempt yet to test the causal story behind the early-career employment decline, and it comes back negative. OECD confirms the phenomenon - the unemployment gap between young labour market entrants and prime-age workers is real and has widened since 2022 across Australia, Canada, the European Union and the United States - but finds no timing, no posting break, and no graduate-specific signature consistent with LLM diffusion being the main driver. It attributes the gap instead to the macro sensitivity of the sectors where LLM-exposed occupations happen to concentrate: information, finance and insurance, and professional, scientific and technical services, all of which cut hiring quickly when capital costs and uncertainty rise. This is the strongest Tier 1 counterweight in the corpus to the Stanford Canaries / Harvard seniority-bias line, and it sits directly against sources already plotted on early-career-employment-decline.
keyFindings: The headline attribution: 'Data from Australia, Canada, the European Union and the United States suggest that the role of LLMs in explaining the unemployment gap of young labour market entrants remains limited, both for those with and without a graduate degree.'

Timing test fails for the AI story. LinkedIn AI-hiring data date the onset of intensive firm LLM use to mid-2023 through early 2024, yet 'no turning point in the unemployment gap trend for college graduates is visible around those dates... in any of the countries analysed.'

Postings test also fails. The ratio of new online postings in top-quintile versus bottom-quintile Language Model Exposure occupations (Felten, Raj and Seamans exposure score applied to Lightcast data) 'exhibits no break at the end of 2023.'

Box 1.6 runs the same test restricted to postings that Lightcast's seniority classifier flags as junior in the United States, and finds no break there either - which is the specific test the seniority-bias hypothesis predicts should show one.

OECD's preferred explanation is compositional and cyclical: LLM-exposed occupations concentrate in information, finance and insurance, and professional, scientific and technical services. These sectors are unusually sensitive to interest rates and uncertainty, and they cut hiring first, which mechanically hits entrants hardest without requiring any AI channel.

The chapter does not dispute the underlying labour-market fact. The entrant-to-prime-age unemployment gap is documented as real and widening across all four economies; the disagreement is purely about cause.

Framing of the broader outlook is that OECD labour markets are moving 'from resilience to risk' - employment has held up but wage growth and hiring momentum are deteriorating, with youth bearing the adjustment.
methodology: Cross-country observational analysis, no experiment and no firm-level identification. Unemployment gaps are computed from national labour force surveys for Australia, Canada, the EU and the US, split by graduate and non-graduate entrants. LLM exposure is measured with the Felten, Raj and Seamans occupational Language Model Exposure score, joined to Lightcast online job postings; the key test is whether the top-quintile-to-bottom-quintile posting ratio breaks at the point when LinkedIn AI-hiring data indicate firms began intensive LLM use. Box 1.6 repeats the exercise on US postings restricted to Lightcast's junior seniority flag. The identification is essentially eyeballing structural breaks in ratio series against an externally dated adoption onset - transparent, but weaker than a difference-in-differences design with a defined control group.
qualifiers: Tier 1, but read it as an attribution finding rather than a magnitude, which is exactly why it enters jobsdata.ai as an overlay rather than a data point: OECD does not produce an estimate of AI-attributable early-career employment decline that could be plotted as a level, and plotting zero would misrepresent a chapter that affirms the gap is real. The absence-of-break method is low-powered - a gradual diffusion effect would not produce a visible turning point, and OECD's own onset dating (mid-2023 to early 2024) is coarse relative to the series. The Felten-Raj-Seamans exposure measure predates modern LLMs and is a capability-overlap construct, so it may mismeasure which occupations are actually affected; results using Anthropic or OpenAI observed-use measures could differ. Posting counts are a hiring-demand proxy, not employment. Finally, this is a four-economy pooled analysis, so it cannot rule out a US-specific effect of the kind the Stanford Digital Economy Lab canaries work identifies in US payroll microdata.
